answer.label: Not George Washington — an unverified line historians call spurious
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording appears in none of Washington’s letters, speeches, or diaries. His estate at Mount Vernon lists it among his spurious quotations, and George Washington scholars find no evidence he said or wrote it. The nearest genuine statement — reported in an 1835 biography, and itself never confirmed as Washington’s — is a different sentence about governing “the universe” without a Supreme Being; it mentions neither “the Bible” nor “a nation.”

source.excerpt: It is impossible to rightly govern the world without God and the Bible.
trail: The Washington estate at Mount Vernon places this line on its list of spurious quotations, noting it is frequently misattributed to Washington, sometimes tied to his 1796 Farewell Address.
PolitiFact rated the attribution False, and a University of Virginia Founders Online editor noted Washington almost never mentioned the Bible in his own correspondence.
The closest documented statement, in James Kirke Paulding’s 1835 biography, has Washington speak of governing ‘the universe’ without a Supreme Being — and even that was never confirmed as his words.
source.excerptNote: Widely shared — often in a “rightly govern a nation” variant, and sometimes padded with an extra fabricated sentence about “separating religion from politics” — but traceable to no document Washington actually produced.
source.rightsNote: No copyright status can be asserted because the wording traces to no identifiable author or first-publication: it is an anonymous modern paraphrase absent from Washington’s public-domain papers. The one near-parallel, in J. K. Paulding’s A Life of Washington (1835), is public domain by age — but it is a different sentence, so it does not establish rights for this popular line.

author.name: George Washington
author.heading: About George Washington
author.bio: George Washington led the Continental Army through the Revolutionary War and served as the first President of the United States (1789–1797). His documented writings — tens of thousands of letters, orders, and diary entries — are among the most thoroughly cataloged of any founder, which is precisely why scholars can say with confidence that this often-shared religious line is not among them. Washington did invoke “Providence” frequently, but rarely mentioned the Bible directly.

misattribution.heading: How a fabrication got pinned on Washington
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-circulated fake Washington quotes — a piety-flavored line with a founder’s name attached and no source behind it.

items.why: His estate at Mount Vernon lists the line as spurious, and it appears in none of his cataloged papers. PolitiFact rated it False.

Paulding’s 1835 Life of Washington reports a distinct sentence — governing ‘the universe’ without a Supreme Being, with no mention of the Bible — that a later paraphraser may have reshaped into the modern quote. Even Paulding’s line was never verified as Washington’s.

A longer form circulating online adds a sentence warning against any “true American patriot” who would “separate religion from politics” — wording with no eighteenth-century pedigree at all, appended to make the fabrication sound like a fuller Washington address.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the sentence is not documented anywhere in Washington’s own words — historians at Mount Vernon classify it as spurious.

context.heading: Why it keeps spreading
lead: The line thrives because it does two things at once: it flatters a founder as devout, and it lends the authority of the first President to a modern argument about religion and government. That combination makes it irresistible for memes, speeches, and social posts — and none of those uses stop to ask for a citation.

What makes it easy to debunk is that Washington’s papers are exhaustively published. When a saying attributed to him cannot be found across tens of thousands of documented letters, orders, and diary entries, the absence is itself strong evidence.
context.pull: A founder’s name, a devout sentiment, and no source — the classic recipe for a fake quote.
